title: Ambapali's invitation
hook: the courtesan invites the Buddha to a meal; he keeps his word even when princes ask later

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Mahaparinibbana, the last journey, began, and your line, meet often, in harmony. Did you reach out to anyone? Today closes a week, and on the road north the Buddha gets two invitations for the same meal. Day five hundred forty-six.

Two chariots race side by side on the road out of Vesali, wheel against wheel, axle against axle. In one, a woman. In the others, a crowd of young nobles in bright clothes, furious. She's just come from the Buddha, who is staying in her own mango grove. She invited him and his monks to a meal tomorrow, and he accepted, by staying silent, which is how he says yes. The nobles are on their way to invite him to the very same meal. They shout: give it to us, and we'll pay you a hundred thousand. Today: Ambapali's invitation.
screen: `TWO CHARIOTS, AXLE TO AXLE.` → `SHE ASKED FIRST.` → `A HUNDRED THOUSAND FOR THE MEAL.`

segments.voice: Ambapali was a courtesan of Vesali, and the Mahaparinibbana Sutta tells her part simply. Her answer to the nobles: even if you gave me Vesali and all its lands, I wouldn't give up that meal. The young men snap their fingers: we've been beaten by the mango woman. Then they drive on to the Buddha anyway and invite him for tomorrow. He tells them he has already accepted Ambapali's invitation. That's all. No speech about status, no lecture about her work. The first invitation stands. The next day, in her own house, Ambapali serves the Buddha and the monks with her own hands. And when the meal is over, she gives her mango grove to the community. The text records the gift plainly, with no comment on who she was. The Elders' Verses of the nuns, the Therigatha, remember her later as a nun herself, with verses on her own aging body attributed to her. Look back at this week. Lohicca told to share what helps. The line of the blind. The trumpeter whose note leaves no one out. Vipassi's four sights. Ananda told, don't say that. The Vajjians who meet in harmony. And now a promise kept, to the person who asked first, whoever she was.
screen: `NOT FOR ALL OF VESALI.` · `BEATEN BY THE MANGO WOMAN.` · `HE HAD ALREADY SAID YES.` · `THE GROVE GIVEN.` · then, large: `FIRST COME, FIRST HONORED.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of a promise you've already made. Something small: a call, a visit, a favor, a meal. Now picture a better offer arriving for the same time. Notice whether it pulls. You don't need to judge that. Just feel what it would be like to keep the first one anyway. Breathe there. After the bell, if there's a promise like that on your calendar this week, honor it. The bell holds the time.
Ambapali's invitation. The courtesan of Vesali who asked the Buddha first; he kept his word when the nobles asked later, and she gave her grove. Today's word.
Your line: first come, first honored. Today, when something shinier shows up, keep the promise you made first. Day five hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Buddhist monastics traditionally accept a meal invitation by silence and keep it once accepted, and lay families across Asia still invite monks to their homes for a meal offering, often to mark a birthday or a memorial.

myth: the Buddha turns down Ambapali's meal when the nobles ask
he tells them he has already accepted Ambapali's invitation.
Ambapali says she wouldn't give up the meal even for all of Vesali
the nobles snap their fingers: beaten by the mango woman.
verses in the Therigatha are attributed to Ambapali
the nuns' verses remember her as a nun, reflecting on her own aging.

fork.setup: you've invited the Buddha to a meal tomorrow. on the road, nobles offer you a fortune to give the meal to them. what do you say?
options: take the money: it's more than a meal is worth.
refuse, even if they offered the whole city.
offer to share it with them.
fork.reveal: Ambapali says not even for Vesali and its lands. the Buddha keeps her invitation too.

original.note: Pali Ambapali: her name contains amba, mango. her grove became a gift to the monks.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha would choose the nobles over a courtesan.
what it means: he keeps the invitation he accepted first, and the text records her gift without judgment.
what a scholar hears: DN 16 places Ambapali's meal and gift of the Ambapalivana at Vesali; Therigatha verses 252–270 are attributed to her.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), Ambapali's invitation and gift

notes: DN 16 paraphrased. Confirm: the Buddha stayed in Ambapali's grove; accepted by silence; the hundred-thousand offer; 'beaten by the mango woman'; the gift of the grove after the meal.
Therigatha verse numbers for Ambapali (often given as 252–270): confirm.
